videos.title: The Real Cost of Running a Wholesale Business (My Actual Numbers)
videos.transcript: Everyone likes to talk about how much money you can make wholesaling a house, including me. But no one ever talks about how much it costs to operate a legit wholesale business and what your actual net profit is at the end of the month or year. In business, it's not what you make, it's what you keep. So, if you're a new wholesaler, by the end of this video, you're going to know exactly what expenses and net profit need to be so that you can build a sustainable business as you grow. And if you're an existing operator, you're going to learn the industry standards so that you can audit your own business and see where you need to make adjustments and improve. All that and more coming up. This video is brought to you by People Leads Pro, the new dispo feature for Propire that makes finding the right buyer for your deals faster than ever before. Instead of wasting time with stale cash buyer lists, People Leads Pro helps you find active buyers and gives you buy boxes and past transactions so you can see what they buy, where they buy, and when they buy. Find better buyers, build better relationships, and move your deals faster. Go to peopleleadspro.com now. Hurry, spots are going fast. Go to peopleleadspro.com to claim your spot. >> Hey, if you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years. And here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. I just reviewed our P&Ls for last month in my Tulsa, Oklahoma wholesale operation with my business partner, Mark Gabriel. In September, we closed seven transactions for a total of $152,576 in gross revenue. Now, we track our metrics and financials meticulously so we can predict with a high level of certainty the number of deals, revenue, expenses, and net profit. Now, this year, we've been averaging around 10 to 11 deals a month. So, we're on track to do about 125 deals or so for the year. So, September was a lighter month with only seven closed deals, but it will serve well to illustrate how to understand and track the financials. At 152,000 in revenue over seven deals, that gave us an average of 21,700 revenue per deal. So, where did all that money go? Now, the first expense that we're going to discuss is advertising and marketing. For the month of September, we spent $39,899 in total marketing or approximately 25% of our revenue over seven deals. That comes to a $5,700 cost per deal. That means our return on ad spend or what's commonly referred to as rorowaz was 3.8. The way to understand rorowaz is for every dollar we spent in marketing to generate leads, we earned $3.8 in revenue. Now rorowaz is one of the most important financial metrics to track in business, especially a wholesale operation. If you're not getting at least 3x rorowaz, you cannot maintain a sustainable wholesale operation. Let me repeat that. If you are not hitting a 3x rorowaz, you cannot build a sustainable business. When it comes to your marketing budget, it should equal 25% of your revenue. That means as a general benchmark, if you earn a 100,000 in wholesale revenue, you should be spending 25,000 in marketing. Now, one of the mistakes I see wholesalers do when they start to struggle is they cut the marketing budget. That's the last expense to cut. I'll keep breaking down the financials, but first, let me tell you a quick story. I recently did a financial audit with a wholesaler in the Metro Detroit market who's been struggling with his wholesale business. videos.transcript: Most wholesalers lose the deal before they ever make an offer. They ask the seller what price they want, immediately start negotiating against that price, only to discover the seller was never prepared to sell their house in the first place. On this video, I'm going to show you a different way to negotiate with motivated [music] sellers. You're going to learn how to get a seller's commitment before negotiating price, [music] how to uncover their real bottom line, and how to negotiate without sounding aggressive, [music] manipulative, or desperate. And best of all, I'm going to give you the exact questions that you need to use [music] on your next seller call. All that and more coming up. >> For a limited time, you [music] can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's motivated seller scripts so you can talk to, email, and text sellers with [music] confidence. Download it now at freeellerscripts.com. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years. And after all these years talking to sellers, I think the biggest mistake most inexperienced wholesalers make is they believe closing a seller means convincing him to accept their offer. That is not your job. Your job is to understand the seller's situation, determine whether you can actually solve their problem, and then help the seller reach a decision. Sometimes that decision will be to do business with you, and sometimes it won't. When you're willing to walk away from deals that don't work, it takes the pressure off of you. And it also takes the pressure off of the seller. And when sellers feel like they're being pressured, they become defensive. When they feel understood and in control, they are more open. They trust you more. And they're much more willing to collaborate. Never forget, distressed sellers often care more about certainty than price. So before you start negotiating price, slow down and focus on understanding the seller situation first. Use a technique called labeling. Labeling is when you repeat back what the seller appears to be thinking or feeling. One way to help you do this is by using it sounds like or it seems like phrases. You could say it sounds like you've been dealing with this property for quite a while. Or it seems like getting this handled without making repairs is important to you. or it sounds like you're concerned that an investor might agree to one price and then try to renegotiate later. Notice that you're not assuming you know or you're not arguing with the seller or defending yourself. Even if you don't agree, you're simply labeling what the seller appears to be thinking or feeling. Then stop talking. Give them the opportunity to confirm it, correct it, or tell you more. Labeling helps you uncover the real reason they're considering selling. Another way to understand the seller's situation is to use a technique called mirroring. Mirroring is when you repeat the last one to three important words the seller said with an upward inflection like a question. For example, if you ask, "What price are you hoping to get for the property?" And the seller responds, "I'd like to get 250,000." A mirror would be 250,000. Then be quiet. Mirroring encourages the seller to share more. He may expand by saying, "Well, that's what Zillow says it's worth." Or, "Well, that's what I paid when I bought it in 2017." Mirroring helps the seller feel safe to share more, such as how he came up with his asking price. If the seller said, "Well, that's what Zillow says it's worth." You could respond by labeling, "It sounds like Zillow's estimate is playing a big role in how you're valuing the property." Then let the seller confirm, correct, or share more. Remember, the point of labeling and mirroring is to help the seller feel seen and heard. So, in turn, he opens up and is more collaborative with you when it comes time to negotiate a deal. Like I said, be careful you don't assume you know what the seller is experiencing. Once you think you've got it, summarize the seller's situation back to him. Say to him, "Let me make sure I understand what's going on. You inherited the property. It's been vacant for 6 months, and you don't want to put any money into it. Your biggest priorities are selling it as is, not paying commissions, and closing before the end of the month. Have I got that right? Now, you want the seller to say, "That's right." Because that's right means they believe you understand them. By the way, that process of making the seller feel safe happens from hello to goodbye. I call it BRT, building a relationship of trust, and it needs to happen through the entire sales process. Now, once you understand the seller situation and you've built a certain level of trust, the next step is to get a commitment from the seller to work with you before negotiating price. Now, I call this the pre-close, and it's one of the most important lessons in this entire video. Write this down. Never spend time negotiating price with someone who isn't willing and able to move forward right now. The idea here is small commitments lead to big commitments. A small commitment to work with you leads to a big commitment to sign a contract with you. Now, the best way to pre-close is by asking what's called nooriented questions. Let me explain what a nooriented question is. Instead of trying to force the seller to say yes, you frame the question so the seller can comfortably say no. For example, instead of asking, "Are you prepared to sign a contract?" I might ask, if we can agree on price and terms that work for both of us, would you be opposed to putting together an agreement today? Now, the correct answer is no. I wouldn't be opposed to that. No, wouldn't be opposed. That means yes, I'm willing to commit. Saying no can help the seller feel safer and move in control, while yesoriented questions can make them wonder what they're being pushed into. But don't stop after asking it once. I like to double tap the commitment. So, if I say, "If we can agree on price and terms, would you be opposed to putting together an agreement today?" And the seller says, "No, I wouldn't be opposed." Then solidify the seller is serious about committing. Ask it again. So, you wouldn't be opposed to putting pen to paper today if we can find something that works for both of us. Now, the reason it's important to ask twice is because the first response could just be a casual agreement. The second question asks the seller to consciously confirm that they are prepared to take action. Keep in mind, you're not getting a commitment to accept your price. You're getting a commitment to make a decision only if you can both reach acceptable terms. That distinction is very important. Once the seller commits to move forward, another important aspect of the pre-close is to verify the seller can actually make the decision to sell. Don't ask, "Are you the only decision maker?" because that can sound threatening. A better way to ask instead is, "Who else would be affected by the sale of this property?" Or another way I like to frame this question is, is there anyone who would be upset if we put a deal together today? Asking it this way gives them room to mention a spouse, a sibling, a business partner, etc. If they say, "I need to discuss it with my wife," you could respond by labeling. It sounds like making this decision together is important. Then ask, "What's the best way for us to include her in the conversation so that everyone has the same information? Is she available now?" Now, whenever possible, get everyone involved before negotiating price. Otherwise, you could negotiate the entire deal and then have to negotiate all over again with someone else. Hey, listen. I know I'm covering a lot of material in this video and it may seem a little overwhelming, but don't worry. I put together a detailed guide which outlines my entire sales process, all the steps, the scripts, what to say, how to overcome objections, and I call it my closer framework. And I'll give it to you for free. Stay to the end of this video to learn how. Okay. So, after the pre-close, finally, it's time to start the negotiation process. Now, before presenting an offer, first get the seller to negotiate against himself. Let me demonstrate how this might look. Let's say the seller's initial asking price was 250,000. At this point in the sales process, I might say something like, "For an ASIS allcash offer with no commissions or cost to you, where we close on your timeline, what would you be willing to take for an offer like that?" Now, by framing it this way, you're essentially soliciting a better price by highlighting the value you're bringing. Now, deliver it calmly and curiously than stop talking. You are giving the seller an opportunity to adjust their own number before you make an offer. They might say, "Well, I might be able to do 235." Now, they just came down 15,000 and you haven't even made an offer yet. Now, you could mirror them 235 where they might say, "Maybe 230,000, but I really couldn't go below that." Then you could respond, "I appreciate you trying to work with me. Is 230,000 the best you can do?" Then you silence again. Most people become uncomfortable with silence and they begin negotiating against themselves. So, don't rescue them by talking. Now, at this point, what do you do if the seller's adjusted price still doesn't work? Let's say the seller comes down to 230,000, but your maximum allowable offer is only 180,000. Start by acknowledging their effort and then ask a very important calibrated question. I call this the how am I supposed to do that question. So, it might sound like this. I appreciate you making an effort to work with me. Let me ask you a question. How do I make this work at 230,000 when the property needs significant work done and renovated properties are only selling for around 275,000 in that neighborhood? When you ask a how am I supposed to do that question, it invites the seller to confront the practical problem you're presenting and help find a solution. The seller might say, "Well, what could you pay?" Which opens the door for you to negotiate a better price. Okay, so after getting the seller to negotiate against himself, now it's time to negotiate the price. The goal is to start low and come up to a price that is satisfactory for both parties. You starting low and coming up is better than the seller starting high and coming down. The idea is that the seller walks away feeling like he worked you up rather than feeling like you worked him down. See the difference? That's why the initial low offer is what we call the anchor price. The anchor price needs to be a ballpark price and it needs to solicit a no. So, how do you do the low anchor? I usually anchor by saying one of two things. I'll say, "In a perfect world, it would be great to be in the low 100s." Another way I like to say it is, I imagine if you got other offers from investors like me, they would be in the high 200s. Now, this is very important. After giving the anchor, shut up. Resist the urge to talk. Let the silence negotiate for you. Don't talk and wait for the seller to respond. Remember, the anchor is a strategic rejection. So, the response should be, "There's no way I could go that low." If they don't say that, you probably didn't anchor low enough. When the seller rejects your anchor price, respond by saying, "Hey, I totally get it. That would be my price in a perfect world. But how close to that price can you get?" And this is where the seller will start to come down on price. Now, after the anchor is rejected, it's time to start the counter process or what I call closing the gap. The goal of closing the gap is to strategically counter back and forth by staying as close to the anchor as you can, but not to exceed the maximum allowable offer. The way this looks is you're going to anchor again slightly up from your initial anchor. So, if your anchor was in the low 100s and your MAO is, let's say, 150,000, you might say, "If I could get closer to the 115 range, how would that sound?" Followed by, "But how close to that can you get?" and continue to repeat the process, slowly coming up, closing the gap. Now, think about it this way. Every thousand dollars I can be under my MAO is another thousand dollar in profit I just made on the deal. So, once you've closed the gap and you're in the profit zone, finally give a firm offer. Say something like, "Hey, I really appreciate you working with me. I would love to put a deal together with you. If you would be willing to put together an agreement today, I would be willing to come up to 138,000. Can we make that happen? And at that point, lock up the deal and get it in writing. Now, I highly recommend you use my nationwide wholesale compliant contracts. I'll give them to you for free. Just go to wholesaler contracts.com for the free download. And like I promised, I'll give you my exact closer framework so that you have it as a blueprint. Use it to follow the steps and the sequences, learn the questions and the proper framing and how to overcome objections. Just go to mycloserframework.com to download it for free. Now, I created this framework as a result of talking to over 10,000 sellers and doing thousands of deals over the past 21 years. The key is practicing and learning how to overcome objections because the more comfortable you are following my closer framework, the easier and faster you'll do deals. So download that now. Go to mycloserframework.com. Now, on this video, I talked about how to close a seller. videos.title: The Ugly Truth About Wholesaling Houses on Zillow
videos.transcript: Did you know that you can wholesale on-market properties that are listed for sale with real estate agents? I've done it hundreds of times, but there are some challenges that can make it more difficult than wholesaling off-market properties. So, in this video, get ready to learn the six biggest challenges wholesaling on-market deals and how to overcome them, coming up. If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years, and here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. In case you don't know, on-market is when a seller hires a real estate agent to list and sell their property. When a property goes on-market, it becomes public and it shows up on Zillow, Redfin, Trulia, and realtor.com for everyone to see. This gets the seller maximum exposure and ideally the highest price the market is willing to pay. In return, the seller agrees to pay commissions on the gross sale price, which is typically 2 and 1/2% for the listing agent and 2 and 1/2% for the buyer's agent for a total of 5 to 6%. Now, the thing is most people, including a lot of real estate investors, think that only unmotivated retail sellers go on-market and you can't find distressed, discounted properties, or motivated sellers on-market, which is just not true. Some sellers look for a cash buyer off-market, and some sellers look for a cash buyer on-market. The reality is every day distressed, motivated sellers list properties for sale with agents, which means that you and me can find these deals, make offers, and get contracts. So, if you're a wholesaler, I want to make something very clear to you. Just because there is an agent representing the seller doesn't change the fundamentals of wholesaling. A contract with a seller is a contract with a seller. It doesn't matter if you're dealing directly with the seller, or an agent is helping the seller, a lawyer is helping the seller, or Donald Trump is helping the seller. Once you have an executed contract with a seller, you now have an equitable interest in the property. That contract is yours to do with as you please. You can perform on the contract and buy the property, or you can assign it to someone else. That's your right. Now, small caveat. There are wholesale laws and regulations, and depending on the state where you're transacting, there could be disclosure requirements, seller right to cancel requirements, licensing requirements, or contract restrictions that impact if and how you wholesale. Now, I cover regulation in detail here on my channel. I also maintain a free report which outlines the regulations in each state. To get that free report, just go to wholesaleregulations.com. So, from here on out, everything I'm going to share is contingent on the rules and laws in your state. So, if you're going to wholesale, it's your responsibility to know, understand, and follow the laws and rules in your state. But, going back to listed properties, the agent's job is to help the seller get an executed contract and see the deal to the closing. That's it. If you decide to assign your contract to someone else, that's on you to find a cash buyer and execute an assignment contract and notify title. It does not involve the agent, and technically, there is nothing the agent can do about it. They may not like it, but at closing, the seller gets exactly what is stated in the contract, and the agent gets their exact commission, same as if you bought the property yourself. Now, having said that, I realize there are some challenges with wholesaling on market properties that are unique that you don't have to deal with when wholesaling off market. So, let's go over the six biggest challenges and how to overcome them. But, first, I want to point out something that I can't iterate enough. And that is that on market lead gen is free. It doesn't cost you anything to find on market deals. That's huge, especially if you don't have a marketing budget. In fact, if you have zero money for marketing, and you want to learn step-by-step how to get your first deal, be sure to check out the video where I break it down in detail. I'll put the link to that video in the description below. Okay, let's cover the six biggest challenges and how to overcome them. Challenge number one is dealing with a difficult agent. Maybe they don't like wholesalers, which is common. Yes, it's true that some agents can make the wholesaling process way more complicated than it needs to be. But just because you have a negative experience with a difficult agent, doesn't mean it doesn't work. Do you know how many complicated, uncooperative, hard to work with, difficult private sellers I've dealt with? Yeah, like most of them. Handle a difficult agent the same way you deal with a difficult private seller, or a difficult lender, or a difficult contractor, or a difficult teenager, or a difficult anybody. Work through the issues as best you can. Now, in the past, I typically wouldn't tell agents that I planned on wholesaling the property. First of all, it's none of their business what I do with the contract. And two, why create unnecessary drama? They would find out eventually at closing, and when they would, I would simply say, "I've got a lot going on right now, so I'm passing this deal on to one of my partners." Partner is referring to your cash buyer. I had an agent get upset one time when they found out at closing that I was wholesaling the deal, and I said to her, "I performed on the contract. We closed on time. The seller got exactly what we agreed in the contract, and you got paid your full commission. What's the problem?" But due to the high regulation environment that we're in, in recent years I've changed that position. I believe it's much better to fully disclose your intent upfront to that agent. I'd rather tell them at the time I'm contracting, or after the contract, but before starting the dispo process. Now, I put together very specific agent scripts that describe how to disclose to agents and overcome these objections. Stay till the end of this video, and I'll tell you how to get that for free. The second challenge wholesaling on-market properties is making sure your contract is assignable. Since the property is on market and there is an agent involved, they will use their state-approved contracts, but you have to make sure that the agent includes the right terms and clauses in the contract so that you can wholesale it. In fact, I created a 10-point offer sheet to provide the agents, which covers all of the essential elements of what needs included in the contract. Now, you simply provide that to the agent so they can make sure everything is included when they write the offer. That's also included with my free agent scripts, so stick around and I'll tell you how to get that for free. But, one of the most important things to make sure is that your contract can be assigned. Now, general rule of thumb is a contract by nature is assignable unless it states in writing that it cannot be assigned. This is called a no assignment clause, which means you would have to do a double closing wholesale and secure what's called transactional funding. Now, this is something my company provides. If you do need double closing funds, go to usejerryscash.com. We even do the first one for free, so check that out. Go to usejerryscash.com to learn more. So, remember, if the contract does not have a no assignment clause, then by default, you can assign it. But, if you want to be extra safe, where you put your name on the contract as the buyer, add the phrase and or assigns, which means you're the buyer or anyone you assign it to. So, if I sign the contract as the buyer using my LLC, Jerry Is a Flipping Genius LLC, I could add {comma} and or assigns, giving me the ability to later assign the contract to a cash buyer. If the contract does have a no assignment clause, such as bank-owned properties, then be sure to follow my workaround strategy using a designated LLC. This technique allows you to do a single closing wholesale, and I did a video that explains it in detail, including all of the paperwork you need. I'll put the link in the description below for you. The third challenge with wholesaling on-market properties is most agents require proof of funds and earnest money, which neither of those things usually come up with private sellers. Let's discuss each one. As a wholesaler, when you make a cash offer, most agents will call you out on that and basically say, "Prove that you have the cash." Now, if you have hundreds of thousands of dollars lying around like me, just show them a recent bank statement and all is good. But, if you don't have liquid cash sitting in a bank account in the amount of your offer, then you can provide a proof of funds letter, which basically says you have a financial relationship with a funding source who can provide you the funds assuming the deal meets certain requirements. A proof of funds letter is equivalent to a pre-approval letter from a lender, and in my experience, this is sufficient for about 90% of agents. And if you're a pro or prime-level subscriber to my wholesaling and house-flipping deal management system, Flipster, you get unlimited custom proof of funds letters for as many offers as you want. That alone is worth the subscription to Flipster. Now, to learn more and test-drive Flipster for free, just go to joinflipster.com. But, what do you do if the agent doesn't like the letter and wants to see hard proof of funds? Here's how to handle that. Tell the agent the following. "My partners and investors I work with can provide a hard proof of funds in the form of a bank statement, just like you want, but I can't ask them for that unless I first have a fully executed contract on the property. So, let's do this. Let's add a contingency clause to the contract that I will provide a hard proof of funds within 10 days of accepted offer." Now, if the agent accepts that contingency, find your cash buyer and get him to provide you a hard proof of funds and use that to provide to your anal-retentive agent. Now, earnest money is also expected with on-market properties. Earnest money is a good-faith deposit held in escrow at the title company and applied towards the purchase and is typically $500 to $1,000, but it could be as high as 10% of the offer price. Now, earnest money is not due until you get an accepted contract. And if you wholesale the deal, you'll get it reimbursed to you on the day of closing. But, I have a lot of people tell me, "Jerry, I don't have a thousand dollars for earnest money." My first response to that is, unlike off-market, which most methods cost thousands of dollars in marketing just to generate leads, finding on-market deals does not cost you anything for marketing. I typically spend three to five thousand dollars in marketing cost per off-market contract. I don't spend a dime with on-market. So, coming up with $500 or $1,000 to float earnest money for a few weeks until I get it back at closing is nothing compared to what you have to spend with off-market. Now, having said that, if earnest money is really an issue, here's a strategy similar to how to handle the proof of funds issue. Put in your contract that you need five or a 10-day inspection contingency for due diligence, and that the earnest money is due at the end of the inspection. Then, find your cash buyer and get him to provide the earnest money. Okay, the fourth challenge wholesaling on-market properties with agents is getting cash buyers access to the property because typically the agent needs to coordinate access with the seller, and in some cases, the agent wants to be present for the showing. So, you can see how that would complicate things with cash buyers. To overcome this, I make sure to address this issue up front. I get the agent to include in the contract in writing at the time of making my offer the following: Buyer to have unrestricted access to the property. Then, only show the property one time to all of your cash buyers. I call this an inspection party, and I did a video that breaks it down in detail, link in the description below. The fifth challenge wholesaling on-market properties is some cash buyers don't like to buy on-market properties. When you take your deal to a cash buyer and he googles the address, he'll see that it's on-market. He won't know your contract price, but he'll see that there's a list price and in some cases, regardless of the numbers or how good of a deal it is, if the wholesale price is anywhere near the list price, the cash buyer might feel like he's not getting a deal. For example, let's say that a property comes out for sale priced really aggressively for 175,000. And let's say that 175,000 is a great price for a flipper. And let's say that if you found the exact same deal off market, your cash buyer would buy it all day long for 175,000. But it's not off market, it's on market, which means nothing other than an agent is involved and it's public. And let's say that you get the contract for 160,000 and you take it to that cash buyer for 175,000. Even though 175,000 is a good deal and it fits his formula, he won't buy it because he feels like it's not a deal because he's paying list price. You see how that's a problem? Let me illustrate using a scenario that happened to me once. I got an awesome on market deal in Philadelphia that came out for sale at 100,000. That was a smoking deal and I made an offer and I got it for 75,000. Then I took it to a local cash buyer I knew that flipped in that neighborhood for 125,000 cash and he accepted. Then he called me back a few hours later and he said he found out that it's on market and listed for 100,000 and now he no longer wants the deal. I said to him, "Why does that matter? If 125 is a deal for you, what does it matter if it's listed on market?" He said, "Because I could have bought it for 100,000. I'm overpaying at 125,000." I said, "But you didn't. I did. Stop counting the money in my pocket and count the money in your own pocket." So, I'll sell it to someone else for 125,000 who didn't care it was listed. But here's the reality, some cash buyers won't care about list price as long as the price fits their formula. Some won't be interested at all just because it's on market and some will be interested only if it's significantly lower than the list price. That way they feel like it's a deal. For example, I just got an on-market deal for 67,000 that was listed for 100,000. Now, I can wholesale that deal all day for 80,000 without much issue because the cash buyer price of 80,000 is significantly lower than the list price of 100,000. So, the cash buyer still feels like he's getting a deal. So, here's what I suggest. Go to your cash buyer who you have a relationship with or find a cash buyer that you can build a relationship with. Tell them that you want to go hard after on-market properties and make a lot of low offers. And tell them the following. If I find an on-market deal and I negotiate a great contract and I bring it to you at your exact buy formula and desired buy price, will you have an issue if it's on market? Solve the problem before it's a problem. And by the way, that's exactly me. I do a lot of fix and flips all over the country and I'm always looking for another deal. So, if you want to be a finder for me, I will pay you $10,000 for every deal that meets my criteria and yes, I will buy on-market deals. To learn how, register for free training and learn all the details, go to my10kcheck.com. Okay, finally, challenge number six, which is the biggest excuse I hear the most with wholesaling on market and that is it's competitive and it's hard to get good deals, which is true. But, since when did we let hard stop us from being successful? So, let me give you three tips for overcoming competition. Tip number one, follow my double dip technique. This is where you do not use a buyer's agent to make the offer and represent you on the transaction. Instead, go directly to the listing agent unrepresented and offer to let her represent you as the buyer. This is called dual agency and it means the listing agent represents both the seller and the buyer and will get both sides of the commission and make twice as much money on the deal. Now, this is very motivating for most agents. Now, some states don't allow dual agency. Now, if that's you, you can still accomplish the same objective by doing designated agency, which is using another agent to represent you in the same brokerage as the listing agent, or the list agent could become what's called a transaction broker, which means they don't represent the seller or the buyer in the transaction and still get both sides of the commission. Now, it's important you present dual agency correctly to agents so they're motivated to work with you. So, I include my double dip technique in my agent scripts that I'll give to you for free, so keep watching. Okay, tip number two is to make the offer as soon as it comes out for sale. My goal is when a distressed property comes out for sale, I call the agent and make my offer within minutes of being listed. The more time that goes by, the more opportunity for other offers to come in. In many cases, speed wins the deal. I've lost deals because I was 5 minutes too late. So, make sure you set up automated noti- -fications. Now, I did a video that shows how to create searches and get these notifications on distressed properties. Be sure to watch that video. Again, I'll put the link in the description. Tip number three is to make a lot of offers. I'm blown away at how lazy most new wholesalers are. Be prepared to make a lot of offers. Yeah, it's work. Yeah, you're going to get a lot of no's. But, if you want to do deals consistently month in and month out, put in the work. I believe the magic number is five offers a day. That's 100 offers a month. If you do that consistently, you will do deals every single month. Remember, the deal of a lifetime comes around about once a week, but you don't get the deal of a lifetime sitting on the sidelines. You get the deal of a lifetime by being in the game, and the way to get in the game is to make offers every single day. Finally, watch a video where I show you how to get agents to bring you distressed properties before they list them for sale. Now, this is huge because now it's off market. So, watch that video now, and I'll see you on the next video.
